transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/time: 2027-12-08 15:00 PST
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Daniel Rivers (CTO, Lucid), Marta Lopez (Head of Platform), Samir Patel (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough): Discussed reliability requirements for Lucid's checkout conversational assistant, multi-region failover and fallback policies, Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs, SLAs and security controls. Agreed next steps: share pricing and schedule benchmarks.

Topics: reliability, incident tolerance, multi-region routing, model fallback/variants, SLA expectations, VPC/private deployment, observability and audit logs.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, that's Priya, our solutions engineer. How's it going?
[00:06] Daniel Rivers: Hey Alex, good, thanks. Busy week but excited to chat about how you handle reliability for our in-app assistant.
[00:12] Marta Lopez: Hi all. Real quick, Samir's on for the SRE perspective. He's got questions about routing and failover.
[00:17] Samir Patel: Yep, hey. I'll jump in mostly on performance and incident tolerance.
[00:20] Priya Shah: Great. Quick agenda: we'll run through how Redwood Hosted/Dedicated/Private behave under incidents, multi-region strategies, fallbacks between model variants, and the kind of telemetry you get in Console. Then Q&A and next steps. Sound ok?
[00:31] Daniel Rivers: Yep. Also want to surface our non-negotiable SLA for checkout flows — 99.95 p99 latency and regional isolation for payments data.
[00:40] Alex Morgan: Perfect — that's helpful. We'll cover routing and SLA guarantees.
[00:44] Priya Shah: So starting with Hosted: we operate multi-region across US and EU and have automatic routing by latency and capacity. If a region has an outage we route to the next healthy region, with an option to prefer regional data residency. In practice for stateless requests that works well but there is a small RTT bump.
[01:05] Marta Lopez: What's a "small RTT bump" in practice? We're targeting 100-150ms for p50, and p99 under 400ms ideally for the assistant.
[01:12] Priya Shah: For Hosted, typical p50 is 80-120ms for our recommended generator model on typical short prompts; p99 can be 300-450ms depending on sequence length. In a cross-region failover you'll see extra network latency — add roughly 50-150ms depending on region pair.
[01:29] Samir Patel: And during a region outage, how do you preserve sessions / KV cache? We rely on prefix caching to avoid regen costs.
[01:36] Priya Shah: Good question. By default KV cache is per-region and sticks with the serving pool. For global session affinity you can enable sticky routing so a session stays in a region; if that region fails you'd lose warm KV and get cold-start behavior. We recommend a hybrid: prefix cache that persists to a central cache for Dedicated/Private deployments. For Hosted we do prefix caching and you can configure a cross-region cache using our Dedicated option or a customer-managed redis in Private.
[02:01] Daniel Rivers: So sounds like Hosted may cause cold starts on failover. We want to avoid that for payments auth.
[02:07] Alex Morgan: Right, for payment-critical flows most customers either use Dedicated capacity pinned to region, or Redwood Private inside their VPC so caches are local. Dedicated gives you reserved pools in region, and we can set up cross-az redundancy. Private gives you full control — your team manages the cache backing.
[02:25] Marta Lopez: If we go Dedicated, what's your SLA? We need an SLA with credit-backed uptime and latency tiers.
[02:31] Priya Shah: Our Dedicated offering comes with an SLA aligned to region availability — typically 99.9% for uptime and latency SLOs we can contract; for higher tiers we have enterprise add-ons for 99.95% and faster incident response. Will need to scope based on capacity commit.
[02:45] Samir Patel: When you say latency SLOs, do you guarantee p99 or p95? We care p99.
[02:49] Priya Shah: We typically guarantee p95 latency in base contracts; p99 SLOs are possible with higher tier commitments and reserved capacity plus specific model pinning and tuning. We'll put those numbers in the pricing/contract.
[03:00] Daniel Rivers: Ok. On the fallback policies — if the primary model is overloaded or OOMs, can Redwood automatically fallback to a smaller quantized variant and keep the semantics? We can't have errors during peak checkout traffic.
[03:12] Priya Shah: Yes — we have automatic fallback chains. For each route you can configure primary model -> fallback model A -> fallback model B. For example gen-xt-large -> gen-large-quant -> gen-medium-quant. Fallbacks can be by cost and by capability. There's also a policy for graceful degradation: you can allow shorter responses or turn off certain steps. The tradeoff is potential quality regression which you track via realtime evals.
[03:35] Marta Lopez: How are fallbacks routed across regions? If a model container fails in us-west-2 and we failover to eu-west-1 and then want to fallback to a smaller model, do you keep the same fallback policy?
[03:45] Priya Shah: Yes, fallback policy is per-route and follows the request wherever it lands. However, model variants available in a region may differ — we maintain a catalog of region-compatible model variants. If a variant is not available in the target region we skip to the next compatible one.
[04:00] Samir Patel: Are there any race conditions where we might get split-brain for rollouts? For example a canary that flips traffic and some hosts revert while others are mid-upgrade?
[04:08] Priya Shah: Our rollout mechanism uses consistent routing tokens. We do canary percentage rollouts and can detect host-level regressions; if a canary fails we automatically rollback at the routing layer to avoid partial split behavior. There's also a health-check and blacklist system so unhealthy hosts are removed quickly.
[04:28] Daniel Rivers: Good. Observability: what do we get in Console for incident diagnosis — token-level breakdown, per-model latency, errors, traces?
[04:36] Alex Morgan: Console shows token-level cost/latency breakdown, per-route model traces, error rates and stack traces for internal failures. We also expose tracing hooks you can ingest into your APM. For Private deployments we can forward logs to your SIEM.
[04:51] Marta Lopez: Audit logs and KMS — we need full audit trails for who invoked what model, and all keys managed through our KMS. How does that work?
[04:58] Priya Shah: For Hosted we provide audit logs with request metadata; for Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and you control keys. Redwood supports envelope encryption with customer-managed KMS. SOC 2 reports and certs we can share — I'll link the compliance pack.
[05:15] Samir Patel: A practical question: during a major incident that takes down a region for an hour, what's the recommended deployment for us? We want minimal user impact for checkout flows and are willing to pay more.
[05:26] Priya Shah: Two patterns: 1) Dedicated per-region, reserved capacity sized for peak + cross-region standby; or 2) Private deployment with active-active across two regions where you control replication for KV cache and state. Dedicated is faster to set up; Private gives maximal control. For mission-critical payments you pick Dedicated+Private hybrid in some customers — Dedicated for core latency-critical endpoints + Private for sensitive auth flows.
[05:50] Daniel Rivers: Hybrid sounds interesting. Can you run a benchmark to show p99 under failover? We need numbers to present to leadership.
[05:58] Alex Morgan: Absolutely — Priya can run a failover benchmark with sample traffic and show p50/p95/p99 comparisons for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. We'll also simulate model fallback to quantized variants.
[06:10] Priya Shah: For the benchmark we'll need a short traffic profile, typical sequence lengths, and any specific request patterns, like long context or streaming responses. Could you share that?
[06:18] Marta Lopez: Yes, we'll share a week of anonymized traffic and a description of checkout-critical routes.
[06:22] Samir Patel: Also want to test canary rollouts under load — prove you won't get split traffic.
[06:27] Priya Shah: We'll include rollout testing in the bench.
[06:30] Alex Morgan: Quick note on private networking: for Private we can deploy inside your VPC with private control plane; we support SAML SSO and RBAC. Does that cover your compliance needs?
[06:39] Daniel Rivers: Yes but need IP allowlist, peering and audit logs forwarded, and KMS integration.
[06:43] Priya Shah: All supported. For peering we do VPC peering and Transit Gateways in major clouds. For on-prem we have an appliance model.
[06:52] Marta Lopez: Another question on throttling during incidents: do you provide graceful throttling or backpressure hooks? We want to implement priority queues for checkout traffic vs low-priority background tasks.
[07:02] Priya Shah: Yes — Redwood routes by policy and supports priority lanes. You can tag routes as high/normal/low and configure token buckets per class; during overload high-priority requests get scheduled first. Also caching reduces upstream hits.
[07:16] Samir Patel: If we tag checkout as high priority, will that impact cost significantly? We're trying to budget.
[07:21] Alex Morgan: Priority scheduling itself doesn't change cost, but reserving capacity for high-priority lanes does. You can set burst capacity and reserved units to balance cost and performance. We'll show cost impact in the pricing deck.
[07:36] Daniel Rivers: On the topic of model variants, how do you validate semantic parity between primary and fallback? We need confidence that fallback doesn't break auth logic.
[07:45] Priya Shah: You can attach prompt tests and evals to a route; during fallback we run lightweight regression checks against a golden prompt set. If degradation exceeds thresholds we can stop routing to the fallback. This is part of Redwood Optimize and the evals pipeline.
[08:02] Marta Lopez: Will that add latency? Running evals in-line may slow things.
[08:06] Priya Shah: The regression checks are asynchronous for the most part — we rely on sampled checks and offline evals. For mission critical flows you can have pre-approved fallback variants with validated pass rates.
[08:16] Samir Patel: How do you handle data residency for audit logs during cross-region failover? Can't have EU data replicated to US for certain flows.
[08:25] Priya Shah: You can mark routes as regional-only where requests never leave the region; in that mode failover is limited and we will return an error rather than route cross-region. Alternatively, for payments you can choose Dedicated in-region or Private.
[08:39] Daniel Rivers: Good — we prefer fail closed for certain PII/payment flows instead of cross-region fallback.
[08:44] Alex Morgan: Noted. We'll mark checkout as regional-only by default in the pilot.
[08:48] Marta Lopez: About incident notifications — do you provide post-incident RCA and customer-facing communications?
[08:53] Priya Shah: For Dedicated customers we have a faster incident response SLA and provide incident timelines, RCA and remediation steps. Hosted customers get notifications via status page and optional webhooks. Enterprise customers get dedicated incident contacts.
[09:06] Samir Patel: During failover, is there support for draining sessions gracefully? Example: sequence generation in-flight when an instance goes down.
[09:14] Priya Shah: We attempt connection draining and persist partial KV where possible, but long-running tokens are inherently tricky. For streaming responses we retry idempotently where possible; best approach is to design idempotent operations and checkpointing.
[09:29] Daniel Rivers: Ok. On logging sensitivity — can we redact sensitive tokens before they hit logs?
[09:34] Priya Shah: Yes, you can configure PII scrubbing rules. For Private deployments you can handle logs entirely in your environment.
[09:41] Alex Morgan: Quick pivot — competitors. Are you evaluating any others?
[09:44] Daniel Rivers: We're looking at OpenAI and Anthropic for model quality, and exploring Bedrock for integration with our AWS infra. Also evaluating self-hosted stacks but worried about ops cost.
[09:55] Alex Morgan: Makes sense. We'll include an apples-to-apples comparison in the follow-up.
[09:59] Priya Shah: Back to technical — network topologies for Private: we can use private control plane model where only telemetry is sent to Redwood control, or completely air-gapped with on-prem packages for higher compliance.
[10:12] Marta Lopez: Air-gapped is interesting but heavier. For now we want VPC + customer-managed KMS.
[10:18] Priya Shah: Good middle ground. For the bench we'll show VPC deployment latency matrix.
[10:23] Samir Patel: On the topic of rollouts, does Redwood provide simulation tools to run canary traffic internally?
[10:29] Priya Shah: We provide a traffic replay tool; you can replay a capture against a new model or new config to measure regressions before going live.
[10:35] Daniel Rivers: Great. Any notes on cost-savings during incidents — like automatically serving cached responses when model is unavailable?
[10:41] Priya Shah: You can configure cache-serving policy: when model is unavailable serve cached best-effort responses subject to staleness limits. Many customers use a hybrid: cached fallback + smaller model + degraded response length.
[10:53] Marta Lopez: For stateful conversational flows we can't serve stale answers for payment verification — needs to be live. So caching is limited for those routes.
[10:59] Priya Shah: Understood; we'll recommend different policies per route.
[11:03] Alex Morgan: We're about halfway — any deeper technical areas to cover?
[11:07] Samir Patel: I'd like to dig into kernel selection and OOM handling under heavy sequence lengths — you mentioned quantization and continuous batching earlier.
[11:15] Priya Shah: Sure. Our runtime picks kernels based on model arch, sequence length and hardware. During high memory pressure the orchestrator will try to switch to quantized kernels and spill KV to disk; if OOM can't be avoided we can restart the shard and route traffic to fallback variants. We also have preemptible spare nodes for Dedicated that take traffic during spikes.
[11:36] Samir Patel: Spill to disk sounds risky. Does that impact latency severely?
[11:40] Priya Shah: It can; that's why for critical flows we size memory and use reserved capacity. Spill is safety net.
[11:46] Daniel Rivers: For the pilot, can we test a simulated OOM and measure our end-user impact?
[11:51] Priya Shah: Yes, we can include OOM and failover scenarios in the benchmark.
[11:55] Marta Lopez: Ok. For contract talks — licensing for Private; is it one-time platform fee plus support, or recurring?
[12:02] Alex Morgan: Private is usually a platform fee plus yearly support and optional on-prem appliance costs. Dedicated is monthly/annual reserved capacity. We'll include pricing options in the deck.
[12:12] Daniel Rivers: On telemetry retention, we need 12 months of audit logs for compliance. Can you support that?
[12:18] Priya Shah: Yes, retention is configurable; longer retention is an add-on. For Private you can forward to your long-term archives.
[12:25] Samir Patel: A note about tracing: do you inject trace ids into token responses or only in logs?
[12:30] Priya Shah: We surface trace IDs and correlate per-request in Console and we can inject them into responses on demand.
[12:37] Marta Lopez: For the benchmark environment, will we be able to run tests ourselves or do you run it and share results?
[12:42] Priya Shah: Both — we can run an initial bench and give you the scripts and capture so you can run in your infra as well.
[12:49] Alex Morgan: Quick recap before we wrap: we'll send pricing and Dedicated vs Hosted comparison, schedule the benchmark, get your traffic profile, and share SOC 2/KMS integration docs. Anything else?
[12:59] Daniel Rivers: Add auditing and regional-only policy config examples to that pack.
[13:03] Marta Lopez: And include sample runbook for failover scenarios.
[13:08] Alex Morgan: Noted.
[13:10] Priya Shah: Any final technical clarifications?
[13:13] Samir Patel: Just one — how fast can you deploy Dedicated capacity in us-west-2? We might need a pilot in two weeks.
[13:20] Alex Morgan: We can provision a small Dedicated pool in 7-10 days typically; for faster timelines we can bolt on burst capacity in Hosted as a temporary measure.
[13:30] Daniel Rivers: Two weeks would be ideal; we'll prioritize the pilot.
[13:34] Alex Morgan: Great. We'll follow up with calendar invites and the decks. Thanks everyone.
[13:39] Daniel Rivers: Thanks.
[13:42] Marta Lopez: Thanks all.
[13:44] Samir Patel: Bye.

Note: transcription has occasional mis-recognition (e.g., "K-V cash" instead of KV cache; "Red wood Console" sometimes), filler words, and speaker labels might be slightly off.

End of meeting.
